title: How Do Veterans Fare in the Civilian Workforce?
gist: RAND podcast with economist Lisa Abraham on a linked Census Bureau (LEHD) study: post-9/11 veterans who enter the civilian labor market at ages 23-35 and stay consistently employed start with slightly lower earnings than comparable non-veterans but see ~10 percentage points more earnings growth over eight years, consistently across gender and race and even after accounting for their lower formal education. Causes are unknown (skills, employer learning, or selection) and the sample excludes federal, self-employed and unemployed veterans.

themes.theme: Veteran earnings catch-up over eight years

insights.claim: Roughly 200,000 service members leave the U.S. military each year, most of whom must find civilian jobs.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A steady ~200k annual inflow of veterans is a structural labor supply source relevant to employers in logistics, security, defense and federal contracting.
insights.quote: On average, roughly 200,000 service members leave the U.S. military each year.

insights.claim: In a RAND study of post-9/11 veterans, veterans started with slightly lower earnings than comparable non-veterans but their earnings grew about 10 percentage points more over the first eight years in the civilian labor market.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Veterans who get through the transition appear to be undervalued at hire relative to later productivity — a potential hiring arbitrage for employers.
insights.quote: veterans’ earnings grow about 10 percentage points more than those of similar non-veterans

insights.claim: Illustratively, two workers starting at $50,000 would reach roughly $85,000 (non-veteran, 70% growth) versus about $90,000 (veteran, 80% growth) after eight years, a $5,000 annual gap that compounds over time.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Translates the growth differential into dollars: a meaningful, compounding wage premium for consistently employed veterans.
insights.quote: the difference at the end of the period is $5,000 a year
insights.locator: Right. Definitely. It’s easy to say

insights.claim: The roughly 10 percentage point faster earnings growth for veterans held broadly consistent across male, female, Black, Hispanic, and white veterans, even though earnings levels differ by group.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: The persistence of the effect across demographics suggests something structural about military experience or selection, not a subgroup artifact.
insights.quote: that pattern of faster earnings growth over time is roughly around 10 percentage points for all the groups

insights.claim: Veterans in the sample had less formal education than non-veterans on average, yet when education is accounted for, their faster earnings growth looks even more notable.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Challenges the degree-centric hiring signal: military training creates uncodified human capital that credential-based screens miss.
insights.quote: when we account for education, the veterans’ faster earnings growth looks even more notable
insights.locator: But what’s interesting in our study

themes.theme: Why veterans catch up: unresolved mechanisms

insights.claim: Abraham's study finds only an association between military service and higher earnings growth; the cause could be skills learned in service, employers learning the value of military experience over time, or selection of the type of person who enlists and stays employed.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Until the mechanism is known, policies or hiring programs built on the veteran premium rest on uncertain foundations.
insights.quote: there’s an association between military service and higher earnings growth in our particular sample, but we can’t say why
insights.locator: Exactly. What we found in this study

insights.claim: Veterans' initial earnings deficit stems largely from a translation problem: civilian employers may not understand how leading teams, managing logistics and working under pressure map to job postings, compounded by decisions about schooling, education benefits, relocation and family.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Skills-translation and credentialing tools for veterans address a real market inefficiency in initial job matching.
insights.quote: civilian employers may not immediately understand how that experience fits into a job posting
insights.locator: Sure, yeah, this is an excellent point

insights.claim: Because veterans appear to have strong growth potential once consistently employed, the transition into the first civilian job is the critical intervention point for support.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Directs policy and corporate veteran-hiring programs toward first-job placement rather than later-career support.
insights.quote: Veterans may need help getting that first job, but once they are in that job and consistently employed, they appear to have strong growth potential.

insights.claim: The RAND study linked two restricted Census Bureau data sets, including the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) data, to follow about 13,000 veterans and 661,000 non-veterans who entered the labor market at ages 23-35 and stayed consistently employed for eight years, controlling for initial occupation, industry and demographics.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Longitudinal linked administrative data ('a movie, not a photo') reveals trajectories that point-in-time surveys miss.
insights.quote: our final sample included about 13,000 veterans and 661,000 non-veterans, roughly
insights.locator: Sure. Yeah. That’s a great question. It’s important

insights.claim: The findings exclude federal employees, self-employed workers, workers in non-participating LEHD states, and veterans who are unemployed or dropped out — a notable gap since veterans enter the federal workforce at disproportionately higher rates.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: The positive result describes a selected, successful segment; it should not be read as evidence that veterans overall outperform.
insights.quote: veterans go into the federal workforce at disproportionately higher rates
insights.locator: And then the last thing I’ll say

insights.claim: Abraham argues the US lacks data infrastructure to track veterans from military occupation specialty through first civilian job to longer-run earnings, and to observe veterans facing underemployment or unemployment, which limits efficient targeting of existing supports.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Better linked military-to-civilian data would enable more efficient targeting of veteran benefit spending; watch for data-linkage initiatives.
insights.quote: it’s about being more efficient about how we’re targeting supports
insights.locator: As an economist, I am always about having more data
